question: Move the AED at P.S. 075 Emily Dickinson into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 075 Emily Dickinson (School, ZIP 10025) has a registered AED at "Outside Room 307; Main Entrance".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.2 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 6 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 9 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists no fire station, police station or hospital within 400 m.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving P.S. 075's AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a documented gap in emergency response. The school's current access—55 hours weekly during the school year, zero hours in summer—leaves the area without nearby defibrillation during 1.2 expected cardiac arrests annually [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. The surrounding area has nine other AEDs but none open 24/7 [E5], and no hospitals or fire stations within 400 meters [E8]. A street-wall cabinet would provide continuous access when it matters most.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on real gaps, but the case for this specific fix is incomplete. Yes, the school's current hours create a problem—1.2 expected cardiac arrests yearly occur when the AED is locked [E4]—and the survival benefit of bystander shock is substantial [E7]. However, we don't know the cabinet's cost, vandalism risk, or whether the school could simply unlock access after hours at no expense [E9]. The nine nearby AEDs, though not currently 24/7, might be relocatable or their hours extended more cheaply [E5]. We also can't confirm those 1.2 calls actually occurred within two minutes of this school rather than elsewhere in the ZIP [E9]. Before installing outdoor infrastructure, we should explore whether unlocking the existing device or coordinating with nearby locations costs less and solves the same problem.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic's point about exploring cheaper alternatives first is fair, but it misses why this specific school matters. The 1.2 annual cardiac arrests occurring during locked hours [E4] represent real people in a documented gap—and that gap is ranked sixth worst among 100 NYC schools, meaning this location has measurable urgency. Yes, unlocking the existing AED would be cheaper [E9], but only if the school agrees and maintains after-hours access reliably. A street-wall cabinet removes that dependency and ensures the 66.5% survival benefit [E7] is available whenever needed, not contingent on administrative cooperation. The nine nearby AEDs being closed 24/7 [E5] suggests the neighborhood lacks institutional will to solve this. A permanent, autonomous cabinet answers the problem directly.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The Advocate makes a fair point about institutional reliability—unlocking the existing AED depends on school cooperation that may not materialize. But that's an argument for exploring the option first, not skipping it. We don't know the cabinet's cost [E9], and if unlocking costs nothing while a cabinet costs thousands, the school might suddenly find the will to cooperate. More importantly, the ranked urgency claim overstates what we know: those 1.2 expected arrests [E4] could have occurred anywhere in the ZIP, not necessarily near this school's entrance [E9]. Before spending on permanent infrastructure, test whether the school will unlock access. If it refuses, then the cabinet case strengthens considerably.

verdict.summary: Documented gap exists (1.2 arrests/year during locked hours, 66.5% survival benefit proven), but cost, vandalism risk, school cooperation feasibility, and precise call locations remain unknown. Test unlocking existing AED first.
verdict.strongestFor: School's current 55 weekly hours creates measurable gap [E4]; bystander shock shows 66.5% survival [E7]; no 24/7 alternatives nearby [E5].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Cabinet cost unknown [E9]; school may unlock existing AED at no cost [E9]; 1.2 calls may not be within two minutes of this entrance [E9]; cheaper alternatives unexplored.
verdict.nextStep: Contact school to test unlocking existing AED after-hours at no cost; if refused, then proceed with cabinet proposal and cost analysis.
